transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Eli Johnson (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Tom Lewis (Head of ML, Acme), Priya Sharma (Eng Mgr), Alex Chen (SRE)

Summary (auto): Quick hosted API walkthrough covering chat/text generation basics, streaming, params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and retry/backoff behavior; addressed security and SSO questions.

[00:00] Eli Johnson: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um I'm Eli from Redwood Inference, and with me is Maya our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Tom Lewis: Hey Eli, doing good, thanks. We are excited to see the hosted API flows, Priya and Alex are on too.
[00:14] Priya Sharma: Yep hi all. Quick timer note we have about 45 minutes.
[00:18] Maya Patel: Great, we'll keep it tight. Quick agenda: 1) show chat demo with streaming, 2) go over key params and cost/latency tradeoffs, 3) retries and failure modes, and 4) next steps. Does that align?
[00:29] Alex Chen: Works for us.
[00:31] Eli Johnson: Cool, starting with a short context question — Tom, could you remind us what you're trying to build? I know you mentioned a fleet operator assistant, edge devices, and some regulatory constraints.
[00:40] Tom Lewis: Yeah right now we want an assistant for operators to triage robot errors and get runbook suggestions. Main constraints: low-ish tail-latency (sub-400ms ideally for common queries), cost needs to scale across thousands of daily sessions, and data must not be stored long-term — some PII scrubbed. We also care about SSO and audit logs.
[01:05] Eli Johnson: Thanks — that helps set parameter choices. Maya, taking over to demo.
[01:09] Maya Patel: Alright I'm going to share my screen. First, simple chat flow using the hosted API — we'll show request, streaming response, then tweak parameters. Apologies if the transcript messes some hostnames, sometimes the auto caption picks up "Dedicate" weirdly.
[01:25] Maya Patel: (screen) Here's a small node script calling /v1/chat/completions. We send a system prompt + user message. Right now model is redwood-jumbo-1 (example).
[01:37] Maya Patel: Sending request... streaming enabled via chunked transfer. You should see tokens arrive incrementally, which helps perceived latency for user.
[01:49] [streaming chunks] Maya Patel: "... and the recommended step is to inspect the battery connector for 2 seconds..."
[01:55] Priya Sharma: Nice, so tokens appear as they're generated. How much of a difference does that make for operator UX?
[02:02] Maya Patel: For human-in-the-loop cases, streaming can cut perceived latency by 30-60% because the user sees immediate partial output. For our metrics we usually measure time-to-first-token vs time-to-complete.
[02:15] Tom Lewis: Time-to-first-token is what we care most about for triage.
[02:19] Maya Patel: Right. Next, parameters: temperature, max_tokens, top_p, n, stop sequences. For deterministic runbooks we recommend temp 0-0.2, max_tokens set to expected length + buffer, and restrict top_p if you want safety. Also show presence_penalty/ frequency_penalty if you get repeated lines.
[02:41] Alex Chen: About cost — is billing per token? How do streaming/chunked responses affect billing?
[02:47] Eli Johnson: Billing is per token generated/consumed; streaming doesn't change cost, it's just a delivery mechanism. So cost is stable whether you stream or wait for full response.
[02:57] Priya Sharma: Got it. What about retries and idempotency?
[03:01] Maya Patel: We recommend client-side retries with exponential backoff for 5xx and 429. For chat endpoints, you can leverage request_id or client message IDs to dedupe. Also Redwood's SDK supports automatic retry hooks with configurable max attempts and jitter.
[03:18] Tom Lewis: If a retry triggers an extra token generation, that would cost us, correct?
[03:22] Eli Johnson: Yes, that's right. So you design retries to avoid duplicate state-changing operations or use short timeouts and conservatively retry only idempotent reads. Another pattern is server-side caching of recent prompts / prefix KV caching to avoid re-generation.
[03:39] Tom Lewis: When you say KV cache, does that mean the platform keeps a cache of key/value representations of the prefix? Any data residency concerns?
[03:47] Maya Patel: The KV cache is ephemeral and tied to the inference instance; in hosted mode we keep it in-memory and it isn't persisted to disk. For regulated workloads you can use Redwood Private and customer-managed KMS.
[03:59] Alex Chen: Do you offer encryption at rest and in transit for hosted?
[04:03] Eli Johnson: Yes TLS in transit, and at-rest encryption for logs and artifacts. We integrate with KMS for key material. We'll share the security whitepaper after this call.
[04:13] Priya Sharma: Great. Can you show parameter changes live — e.g., increase temperature and show variability?
[04:18] Maya Patel: Sure. Changing temp to 0.8 now, re-sending same prompt.
[04:25] [streaming chunks] Maya Patel: "... you might try recalibrating the torque sensor, but another approach is to reroute commands through safe mode..."
[04:33] Priya Sharma: Hmm that looks more creative, we prefer deterministic.
[04:36] Maya Patel: Yep, that's expected. For deterministic outputs use temp 0-0.2 and set max_tokens tightly. Also consider a smaller model variant if you only need concise runbook steps.
[04:49] Tom Lewis: What about latency numbers for models?
[04:53] Eli Johnson: We publish benchmarks per model. For redwood-jumbo-1 at 256 context typical p50 is ~70-120ms on our hosted infra, but p95 depends on payload and batching. If your tail requirements are strict we can run a targeted benchmark via pilot.
[05:10] Alex Chen: You mentioned batching earlier — how does that affect latency for real-time agent queries?
[05:15] Maya Patel: Continuous batching will aggregate requests to increase throughput and lower cost. For low-latency SLOs you can disable large batching or use dedicated capacity. Redwood hosted offers latency-aware routing: small customers get lower batch windows.
[05:30] Tom Lewis: If we hit spikes, is there automatic fallback to a cheaper model to preserve availability?
[05:35] Eli Johnson: Yes we can configure routing policies to fall back to smaller model variants or to different regions. We also support graceful degradation like returning short summaries instead of long responses.
[05:46] Priya Sharma: How about quota and rate limits?
[05:49] Eli Johnson: Host tier has per-account rate limits; for production we typically put you on a committed tier or dedicated pool which removes noisy neighbors and sets guaranteed throughput.
[05:59] Tom Lewis: For pilot we likely want hosted but with a reserved burst capacity.
[06:04] Maya Patel: Totally doable. We'll include that in the pricing deck.
[06:08] [06:08] Quick aside about tooling
[06:09] Maya Patel: Now show retry example — here's a curl hitting the chat endpoint and we simulate a 503 by dropping connection; client retries with backoff, we show idempotency header to avoid double-billing.
[06:23] [Example code readout] Maya Patel: "X-Request-ID: 12345" and we show server response 200 when deduped.
[06:30] Alex Chen: So the header is honored server-side?
[06:33] Maya Patel: Yes we support dedupe windows for requests when given id. It's not infinite retention, but enough to cover retries.
[06:40] Tom Lewis: What about streaming interruptions mid-response — can client resume?
[06:44] Maya Patel: We don't currently support resuming a partial stream from the exact token index on hosted, you would need to replay the prompt but with caching improvements we can reduce repeat work. For on-prem/Private deployments we have options for more advanced session resume.
[06:59] Priya Sharma: Understood. Any details on observability — how do we trace tokens to costs?
[07:05] Eli Johnson: Console has token-level cost breakdown, per-route and per-user. You can attach metadata like workspace IDs, and we surface traces to pinpoint high-cost prompts.
[07:18] Tom Lewis: Great. Security — SSO, audit logs?
[07:21] Eli Johnson: SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC, audit logs are available for enterprise customers. We'll attach the SOC2/ISO documents to the email.
[07:30] Priya Sharma: Ok good.
[07:32] Maya Patel: Next, quick demo of streaming with function/tool calling — simplified example calling a tool to fetch telemetry.
[07:40] [demo] Maya Patel: You can see structured output come in, then our SDK can map to UI components.
[07:50] Tom Lewis: That structured output is useful for automating runbook execution.
[07:54] Maya Patel: Exactly — we can return JSON and signpost confidence.
[08:00] Alex Chen: On the topic of PII scrubbing, do you provide built-in scrubbers?
[08:05] Eli Johnson: We have options: client-side masking, Redwood pre-processing hooks that mask certain patterns, and enterprise retainers for redaction. We'll include docs.
[08:16] Priya Sharma: Anything about data retention windows for hosted?
[08:19] Eli Johnson: Hosted API logs are retained per-account policy; for stricter requirements you can choose Private which gives you control over retention.
[08:27] Tom Lewis: For pilot we need 30-day retention then purge, yes.
[08:31] Eli Johnson: Noted.
[08:33] Maya Patel: Last demo bit — tweaking max_tokens to limit hallucinations, plus stop sequences for structured outputs.
[08:40] [demo send] Maya Patel: Response truncated to stop sequence, shows less hallucination.
[08:48] Priya Sharma: Works well.
[08:51] Tom Lewis: Any rate-limiting guidance for our client-side SDK? Like do you recommend circuit breaker patterns?
[08:56] Maya Patel: Yes use circuit breakers + exponential backoff + token-aware budgeting. Our SDK has hooks for all these.
[09:04] Alex Chen: For the pilot test — we'll want to run a 1k concurrent user sim, how do you recommend benchmarking?
[09:09] Maya Patel: We'll give you a lightweight script that scales clients across multiple machines, measure time-to-first-token and p95. I'll attach it.
[09:17] Tom Lewis: Cool.
[09:19] Eli Johnson: Quick recap and open Qs — Priya anything blocking on legal/compliance?
[09:24] Priya Sharma: We need SOC2 + network diagrams and KMS options; otherwise we can start pilot.
[09:29] Eli Johnson: We'll send those.
[09:31] Tom Lewis: Pricing model question: committed vs pure pay-as-you-go?
[09:35] Eli Johnson: We offer both; committed (Dedicated) gives discount and reserved throughput. Hosted pay-as-you-go is flexible for pilots. We'll include an example cost model based on your 1000 concurrent assumption.
[09:47] Priya Sharma: Great.
[09:49] Maya Patel: Any other deep technical asks?
[09:52] Alex Chen: Would like to see p95 numbers under our payload distribution — that's the benchmark step.
[09:57] Maya Patel: We'll run that in pilot.
[10:00] Eli Johnson: Ok next steps recap: Eli to send pricing and security docs; Maya to send benchmark script and postman collection; Tom to share prompt set and SLOs; schedule pilot kickoff.
[10:12] Tom Lewis: Sounds good. Thanks, that was helpful.
[10:16] Priya Sharma: Thanks all.
[10:18] Eli Johnson: Thanks everyone, we will follow up by EOD with material and proposed times for pilot kickoff.
[44:10] (call ends)

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts — e.g., "K V cash" instead of KV cache, "Redwood Dedicate" vs Dedicated. Speakers sometimes overlapped; auto transcript includes filler words.
